A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SEM-CTRL and support reliable comparison of their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Material can be matched across the expanded and reorganized appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original grammar-synthesis, combinatorial-reasoning, and Blocksworld experiments, including ablations and additional results in Appendix F.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds reasoning-model comparisons, JSON evaluation, and a fine-tuning study, with further results in Appendix H.

M1.justification: ASG-constrained token selection, domain-reward-guided MCTS, greedy rollouts, and caching/pruning strategies remain unchanged. Both versions already describe many-to-many vocabulary alignment, although its mathematical formalization changes. The JSON and fine-tuning experiments reuse existing decoding modes.

E1.justification: v3 adds NousResearch JSON-mode evaluation: extracting natural-language information into schema-conforming JSON. This extends coverage to semi-open-ended structured generation without semantic constraints or correctness rewards. The original grammar-synthesis, Sudoku, graph-coloring, and Blocksworld tasks remain.

E2.justification: DeepSeek-R1 and o4-mini join o1-preview in the original benchmark comparisons and appendix results. XGrammar is evaluated on JSON in v3 Table 5. Conversely, the six Beam comparator rows in v1's combinatorial-reasoning ablation Table 13 disappear from the corresponding v3 Table 15.

E3.justification: New protocols include single-generation, Base-only JSON evaluation and fine-tuning Llama 1B with 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, and 100% of PlanBench training data. The latter uses the existing 50-problem ablation set and adds sampled sequences before solution as an efficiency metric. Original-task sampling budgets and evaluation settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: Section 5.6 and Table 6 add a substantial sensitivity study of fine-tuning data quantity, testing its effects on accuracy and MCTS sampling effort against greedy decoding. The original constraint/search ablations remain, apart from the removed Beam comparisons in the combinatorial-reasoning appendix.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports paired permutation tests at alpha = 0.05 for Blocksworld comparisons in Section 5.1. Three-run averaging, its Blocksworld exception, and soft-accuracy standard-deviation reporting already appear in v1; no increased repeated-run count is established.

E6.justification: v3 adds JSON validity, fine-tuning accuracy/efficiency, and DeepSeek-R1/o4-mini results. Table 6 reports 90% accuracy for SEM-CTRL with Llama 1B at 20% fine-tuning data. Most retained scores are unchanged, but 70B Blocksworld accuracy changes from 96.7% to 96.8%; Table 4 changes its token count from 588.4 to 589.3 and constraint time from 35.94 to 35.97. Beam ablation results are removed.

T1.justification: Equation 5 generalizes vocabulary alignment from individual terminals T to terminal sequences T*. v3 also corrects prefix/action arguments in the validity argument and reward/PUCB expressions, and adds the runtime decomposition in Equation 9. The underlying ASG definitions and validity argument remain, without a new theorem or substantial new proof.

C1.justification: The abstract replaces guarantees of correct completions and solution correctness with valid completions and semantic validity, narrowing the headline guarantee toward the distinction already present in v1's method section. The ASG-plus-MCTS and parameter-efficiency contributions remain, while broad output-correctness language persists in the introduction.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive discussion of ASG-authoring expertise, unsupported logics, and worst-case constraint-checking complexity. Section 5.4 qualifies token counts as a cost proxy given unknown baseline hardware. Sections 5.5–5.6 add interpretations of CFG-only equivalence and complementarity between fine-tuning and search, substantially expanding applicability and mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds illustrative Sudoku, Blocksworld, and JSON ASG encodings, and Section 2 identifies Lark as the source of the JSON grammar. A new footnote promises code release after acceptance or review completion. Existing hardware specifications, sampling budgets, and prompt templates are largely retained; detailed fine-tuning hyperparameters are not supplied.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around explicit CSG control and global correctness optimization, including a new first-direct-CSG-use claim. It adds discussion of XGrammar, IterGen, Loula et al., ASP applications, and LLM-generated ASP, while removing references including Guidance and Willard–Louf. These changes go beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: Retained material is extensively rewritten, particularly the introduction, ASG background, method explanations, and results discussion. Results subsections become research questions, baseline descriptions expand, and the appendices separate ASP background from grammar examples and add a dedicated baseline-methods section.

P2.justification: v3 adds a grammar/parse-tree illustration, three additional grammar-example figures, and JSON/fine-tuning tables. The original grammar example survives as Figure 7 and is also incorporated into Figure 2. Tables 2–4 now sit beside prose, and appendix ablation tables are substantially rearranged and compressed.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, v3 makes the framework and its competitiveness easier to assess through clearer ASG explanations, practical limitations, additional baselines with paired tests, and JSON/fine-tuning evidence. The gain is limited by new weaknesses: Section 3.2.2 does not justify tractable enumeration of T* from finite T, and Section 5.6 uses Table 6's 100%-data search cost to support a claim about 20–50% fine-tuning.
